strengths: The paper addresses an important problem through a useful ASR benchmark with natural speaker-level heterogeneity, domain shift, and a constrained number of communication rounds.

Per-layer clipping produces substantial empirical gains. In Table 1, at σ_DP=3×10⁻⁶, test WER improves from 31.1% with global clipping to 21.2% with uniform per-layer clipping and 20.4% with dimension-based clipping.

The extensive experiments cover initialization, cohort size, optimizers, data heterogeneity, three languages, and multiple model sizes. The diagnostics of layer-wise update imbalance provide useful empirical insights beyond simply combining existing techniques.

Public datasets, detailed training configurations, compute reporting, and a linked code release support reproducibility. The authors explicitly disclose the extrapolation assumptions and limitations; no separate serious research-ethics issue is apparent.
weaknesses: The central convergence claim is not established as stated. Corollary 1 requires κ=1−8(1−η_loc T_loc)²>0 while choosing η_loc=Θ(1/(L√(T_loc T))). For fixed T_loc, this makes κ approach −7 as T increases, invalidating the claimed asymptotic convergence argument. The displayed bound also retains a nonvanishing DP-noise term.

The proof contains additional substantive gaps. Equations E.32–E.33 treat the adaptive scaling p_h^(t) as independent of current DP noise, although Equations E.9–E.14 compute it from the noisy aggregate. Equation E.19 also infers uniformly bounded gradients from smoothness without establishing the additional bounded-domain or bounded-gradient assumption. These issues weaken the claimed rigorous explanation of the method.

The privacy accounting needs a consistent mechanism specification. Algorithm 1 describes Bernoulli client sampling but implements fixed-size cohorts. Moreover, Appendix H.1 asserts equivalence between client-side and server-side Gaussian noise; under Bernoulli sampling, the aggregate client-side noise variance depends on the realized cohort. Applying the standard sampled-Gaussian accountant therefore requires justification beyond matching expected variance.

The headline privacy–utility pairs are conditional projections. Table 1 measures WER with 34,753 users and cohorts of 1,024, whereas the highlighted ε=4.5 and ε=7.2 results require approximately 7 million and 70 million users, respectively, with cohorts of 204,800. The larger-cohort experiments in Table 16 omit DP noise and reach only 5,120 clients. The disclosed extrapolation is informative, but its accuracy and deployment feasibility remain insufficiently validated.

The claimed interaction between LAMB and per-layer clipping is not adequately isolated. Tables 8–9 compare optimizers without DP, while the main noisy comparisons use LAMB throughout. A matched comparison of Adam/LAMB and global/per-layer clipping under identical privacy and tuning budgets is needed to substantiate the proposed mechanism, particularly because both components are established techniques.

Some generality claims exceed the results. Appendix H.7 states that per-layer clipping consistently outperforms global clipping across model sizes, but Table 21 reports worse WER for the deep model: 26.4% versus 25.7%. Gains are also marginal for French and German. Missing repeated-run uncertainty estimates make these smaller differences difficult to interpret.
